title: Stoichiometry and reaction types
note: Coefficients in a balanced equation are mole ratios. To get from grams of one substance to grams of another, convert grams to moles, use the mole ratio, then convert back to grams. The limiting reactant runs out first and sets the theoretical yield. Most reactions fall into a few classes: precipitation, acid–base, and oxidation–reduction (including combustion and single displacement).

read.title: From a balanced equation to grams
text: A balanced equation is a recipe written in moles. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to give two moles of water. The coefficients are not masses: two grams of hydrogen do not react with one gram of oxygen. To work with masses, convert each one to moles with its molar mass, use the mole ratio from the equation, and convert back to grams at the end.

Real mixtures rarely contain reactants in exact ratio. Suppose you mix 2 mol H₂ with 2 mol O₂. The hydrogen needs only 1 mol of oxygen, so hydrogen runs out first. It is the limiting reactant, and it alone decides how much water can form: 2 mol, or about 36 g. That calculated amount is the theoretical yield. The 1 mol of oxygen left over is the excess reactant.

In the lab you usually collect less than the theoretical yield. Some product is lost in transfers, and side reactions may consume reactants. Percent yield compares what you got to what was possible: actual yield divided by theoretical yield, times 100%. A yield above 100% does not mean you beat chemistry; it usually means the product is still wet or impure.
